The first and clearest case is where, in the absence of a legislative 
rule by the agency, the legislative basis for agency enforcement 
would be inadequate. * * * Section 14(b) [of the Securities 
Exchange Act], for example, forbids certain persons, “to give, or to 
refrain from giving a proxy” “in contravention of such rules and 
regulations as the Commission may prescribe.” The statute itself 
forbids nothing except acts or omissions to be spelled out by the 
Commission in “rules or regulations.” * * *
Second, an agency seems Ekely to have intended a rule to be 
legislative if it has the rule pubhshed in the Code of Federal 
Regulations; 44 U.S.C. § 1510 Emits pubEcation in that code to 
rules “having general appEcabiEty and legal effect.”
Third, “ ‘[i]f a second rule repudiates or is irreconcilable with 
[a prior legislative rule], the second rule must be an amendment 
of the first; and, of course, an amendment to a legislative rule 
must itself be legislative.’ ”
American Mining Congress has been much praised. See, e.g., Richard 
J. Pierce, Jr., Distinguishing Legislative Rules from Interpretive Rules, 52 
Ad min . L. Re v . 547 (2000). Indeed, the case is of great practical utiEty 
because it Ests some common “red flags” that clearly identify a rule as 
legislative rather than interpretive. (Note though that the D.C. Circuit has 
since deleted pubEcation in the C.F.R. from this Est of red flags. Health 
Insurance Ass'n of America, Inc. v. Shalala, 23 F.3d 412, 423 (D.C. Cir. 
1994).)
But however useful its red flags are, American Mining Congress has 
not been the last word on interpretive rules. Although the presence of a red 
flag—such as the rule’s necessity to an agency enforcement action or the 
rule’s inconsistency with a prior legislative rule—is sufficient to make a 
rule legislative, American Mining Congress does not say whether the 
absence of a red flag is sufficient to show that a rule is not legislative. This 
has left open the door for later D.C. Circuit cases to elaborate on the 
distinction between legislative and interpretive rules.
Perhaps the most important of those later cases. Paralyzed Veterans 
of America v. D.C. Arena L.P., 117 F.3d 579 (D.C. Cir. 1997), concerned the
